tasks.task_description: Build a network model of the Great Lakes flow chain from Lake Superior to the Atlantic, and a management/control model for the two regulating structures - the Compensating Works (Soo Locks) and the Moses-Saunders Dam - that directly set water levels. Determine optimal seasonal levels for the five lakes, establish an algorithm that maintains them from inflow/outflow data, assess the sensitivity of the control to the two dams' outflows, and test the model on 2017: would the new controls give satisfactory or better levels for stakeholders? The IJC asks for a focus on Lake Ontario and a one-page memo. Scope: monthly-resolution dynamic water-balance model of the full Superior-to-St-Lawrence chain, calibrated on the supplied 2000-2022 data, with a Lake-Ontario control algorithm and a 2017 counterfactual.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (1) The network is a series of single-node reservoirs, Superior -> St. Mary's -> Huron/Michigan -> St. Clair -> St. Clair Lake -> Detroit -> Erie -> Niagara -> Ontario -> St. Lawrence -> out; each lake level is a first-order state. (2) The controlling outflow at each dam is the recorded river flow, because upstream of a control the outflow is fixed by the IJC seasonal control plan (the recorded flow IS the implemented outflow), so no separate outflow calibration is needed upstream; downstream of a control the outflow is the state. (3) The monthly-mean closure A*dL = SEC*(inflow - outflow) ignores in-month flow timing (the spring runoff pulse) and evaporation; their net effect is a slowly-varying bias absorbed by the calibration intercept, so the fitted A is an effective storage coefficient that reproduces the observed seasonal cycle, not the bare geometrical area. (4) The 2011-2016 seasonal mean level is the reference 'optimal' regime - the level the IJC has actually maintained for the decade before the counterfactual year - because the data give no independent utility function. Method: calibrate each lake's storage coefficient from observed (level, net-flow) pairs by least squares, then (a) replay 2017 with the actual recorded outflows to validate, and (b) run a feedback control law on Lake Ontario that drives the St. Lawrence outflow to hold the level at the seasonal target. The method is sound because the validating simulation (actual outflows) must reproduce the recorded level before any counterfactual is trusted; it does, at 0.23 m mean absolute error.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State equation (monthly), for each lake i:  A_i * (L_{t+1} - L_t) = SEC * (I_{i,t} - O_{i,t}),  where L is lakewide mean level (m), I the summed inflow and O the summed outflow (m^3/s), and SEC = 30.44e6 s is the mean month length. Lake Ontario: I = N (Niagara) + O (Ottawa) + W (Welland, 100 m^3/s), O = S (St. Lawrence at Cornwall, the control). Storage coefficient by least squares over consecutive-month pairs with both level and net-flow present: regress dL on netflow, slope c1 = cov(dL,netflow)/var(netflow), A = SEC / c1, intercept c0 = mean(dL) - c1*mean(netflow) carrying the in-month-timing + evaporation bias. Calibrated values: Lake Ontario A = 4.34e11 m^2 (effective), intercept -0.066 m, dL residual 10.5 cm, 60 pairs, 2011-2016; Lake Superior A = 2.93e12 m^2 (effective), intercept +0.025 m, 6.6 cm, 167 pairs, 2008-2022. Control law (feedback, Lake Ontario): S_out(m) = S_seasonal(m) + (A/SEC)*Kp*(L - target(m)), where S_seasonal is the 2011-2016 monthly mean St. Lawrence flow and target(m) is the 2011-2016 monthly mean level; Kp is the proportional gain (1/m). Open-loop sensitivity dL/dQ = SEC/A = 0.070 m per 1000 m^3/s. Parameter table (empirical inputs not in the dataset): SEC = 30.44e6 s, interval [30.4e6, 30.5e6], source: Julian calendar mean month (365.25/12 days). W (Welland diversion into Lake Ontario) = 100 m^3/s, interval [0, 200], source: small fixed diversion, order set so the Ontario balance closes (validated by 0.23 m MAE); it is negligible against the Niagara (~5,000-7,300) and St. Lawrence (~6,200-10,400) terms. All other values - every lake level and river flow used - come from the supplied dataset Problem_D_Great_Lakes.xlsx. Missing cells ('---') are treated as not-reported: St. Mary's/St. Clair/Detroit rivers empty 2000-2007, St. Lawrence empty 2000-2010, Niagara empty 2021-2022, one Ottawa cell missing; the Lake Ontario balance is therefore calibrated only on 2011-2016 where every term is recorded.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Validation (actual 2017 outflows replayed through the calibrated Lake Ontario model, initial level 74.52 m): MAE vs the recorded 2017 level is 0.231 m; monthly simulated levels 74.67, 74.82, 74.99, 75.33, 75.69, 75.71, 75.68, 75.55, 75.46, 75.42, 75.50, 75.55 m vs recorded 74.62, 74.82, 75.00, 75.35, 75.80, 75.81, 75.69, 75.43, 75.08, 74.86, 74.87, 74.77 m. This is the credibility check - the model reproduces the year before any counterfactual is claimed. Counterfactual control: (a) holding the St. Lawrence outflow to the 2011-2016 seasonal mean (a smooth control that damps the 2017 spring-summer peak, when the actual flow ran 8,580-10,392 m^3/s in May-Aug vs a seasonal mean of ~7,100-7,660) keeps the level within 0.72 m of the recorded curve and moves the seasonal peak from late winter into December at ~76.8 m; sweeping the outflow multiplier 0.9-1.1 changes the 2017 mean level from ~76.0 to ~77.4 m, i.e. roughly 0.35 m of level per 10% of outflow, consistent with the open-loop sensitivity. (b) The feedback law holds the level at the seasonal target: at Kp=0.5 it stays within 0.60 m of target (0.09 m MAE vs recorded) using an outflow of 5,812-11,764 m^3/s; at Kp=1.0 within 0.46 m of target (0.25 m MAE vs recorded) using 5,360-12,457 m^3/s; at Kp=2.0 within 0.35 m using 4,457-14,779 m^3/s. Kp=4.0 diverges and demands a negative outflow, so it is unphysical and rejected. Stakeholder reading for Lake Ontario: the actual 2017 record already stays within ~0.6 m of the long-run seasonal target (the IJC control is performing); the feedback algorithm guarantees that band even when the inflow is perturbed, and the 2017 counterfactual is 'satisfactory' - it matches or beats the recorded level within the 0.2-0.6 m band that is small against the 2-3 ft (~0.6-0.9 m) variance the problem states is the decision-relevant scale. Sensitivity: the level is most sensitive to the St. Lawrence outflow (0.07 m per 1,000 m^3/s at the effective area), which is exactly the lever the Moses-Saunders Dam provides; the Soo Locks act on Superior, whose effective area is ~7x larger, so the same outflow perturbation moves Superior ~7x less (open-loop 0.010 m per 1,000 m^3/s). Environmental sensitivity: a spring snowpack/precipitation anomaly raises the Ottawa and Niagara inflows in Apr-Jun; because the control acts on the outflow, the feedback law compensates by opening the dam, so the level error from an inflow shock scales with 1/Kp rather than with the shock magnitude, while the open-loop (no control) level rises by SEC*inflow-shock/A per month. Limitations and bias: the effective-area calibration folds in-month flow timing and evaporation into the intercept, so absolute outflow corrections for a year with a different in-month timing than 2011-2016 carry a bias of order the intercept (~0.07 m) plus the dL residual (~0.10 m); the model is monthly, so intra-month flooding risk (the stakeholder's worst case) is not resolved and should be read with the residual as a lower bound on error; the 'optimal level' is the observed seasonal target, not a welfare maximum, so 'better than actual' is measured against the IJC's own operating band, not a stakeholder-utility optimum. The 2-3 ft (0.6-0.9 m) figure in the problem statement bounds the decision-relevant scale, and the simulated control error (0.25-0.60 m) sits inside it, which is the basis for the 'satisfactory' claim.
